implementation_notes: The BCL supplies the carrier: pass a CancellationToken through every asynchronous API and arm the request's token with CancellationTokenSource.CancelAfter(remaining) so the budget expires on schedule. On ASP.NET Core gRPC the incoming deadline arrives as ServerCallContext.Deadline (a UTC instant, as gRPC defines it) and the call's lifecycle token as ServerCallContext.CancellationToken; the gRPC client factory with EnableCallContextPropagation() copies both onto child calls automatically and resolves competing budgets by taking the smallest deadline. Outside gRPC the same shape is built with CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource(parent) plus CancelAfter(remaining), so a hop's token dies either with the caller or with the budget.
pitfalls: CancellationToken is cooperative: every async database or HTTP call must receive it (pass the token down) or it runs to completion after the deadline - the gRPC runtime aborts the call, not your Task.
CancellationTokenSource and linked sources must be disposed; an undisposed linked source keeps the parent registration and the timer alive.
CallOptions.Deadline is an absolute UTC instant, so copying it between machines assumes synchronized clocks; the wire protocol converts it to remaining time, so never serialize DateTime yourself.
Cancellation surfaces as OperationCanceledException/TaskCanceledException, not as DeadlineExceeded - map the two deliberately so callers can distinguish cancellation from infrastructure failure.

EnableCallContextPropagation() takes the smallest available deadline: a child call's larger explicit deadline is not preserved, and a smaller explicit one wins - know which side you are on when mixing manual and automatic propagation.

Guard the CancelAfter arithmetic: the method rejects out-of-range delays (below -1 ms or beyond the supported maximum), so clamp the computed remaining TimeSpan and fail fast when it is already <= 0 instead of arming a broken timer.
